items.name: OS Hardening Guidelines
items.summary: Defines the mandatory hardened build state for every operating system instance the carrier runs, so servers and workstations enter production with a consistent, attack-resistant configuration that can be measured and enforced over time.

subs.title: CIS Benchmarks Applied
subs.description: Every operating system image must be configured against the applicable Center for Internet Security (CIS) benchmark at the level designated for its environment tier. Deviations from benchmark recommendations require a documented justification and risk acceptance, and benchmark compliance scores are reported through the configuration management tooling.

subs.title: Unnecessary Services Disabled
subs.description: Builds must remove or disable any service, daemon, protocol, or default account not required for the system's documented business function, reducing the attack surface exposed to the network. Service inventories are reviewed when a system's role changes and during periodic configuration audits.

subs.title: Secure Configuration Baseline
subs.description: A version-controlled baseline defines the approved settings for each supported OS platform, and all production hosts are checked against it for drift. Changes to the baseline follow change management, and systems found out of compliance are remediated or formally excepted within defined timeframes.

items.name: 72-Hour Incident Notification
items.summary: Requires the carrier, as a New York licensed entity, to electronically notify the NYDFS superintendent no later than 72 hours after determining that a reportable cybersecurity incident has occurred at the company, an affiliate, or a third-party service provider. The obligation continues after the initial filing, with a duty to promptly update the superintendent as material new information about the incident becomes available.

items.name: Access Privileges & Management
items.summary: Implements the access-control requirements of 23 NYCRR 500.7, governing how user and privileged access to information systems holding nonpublic information is granted, constrained, reviewed, and revoked. The standard ensures access across the carrier remains limited to what each person's job requires and that elevated rights cannot accumulate unchecked.

subs.title: Enforce Least Privilege
subs.description: User access to information systems containing nonpublic information must be limited to the minimum necessary for the individual's job function. Entitlements are granted through role-based provisioning rather than ad hoc assignment, and broader access requires documented business justification.

subs.title: Limit Privileged Accounts
subs.description: The number of privileged accounts must be kept to the minimum the business requires, with each account scoped to the specific functions it supports and used only when performing those functions. Routine work is performed under standard accounts, and privileged sessions are restricted to administrative tasks.

subs.title: Annual Access Review and Removal
subs.description: All user access privileges, including privileged accounts, are reviewed at least annually, and any access found unnecessary for the holder's current role is removed. Review results, decisions, and remediation actions are documented as compliance evidence.

subs.title: Disable Remote-Control Protocols
subs.description: Remote-control devices and protocols that allow remote command of internal systems must be securely configured or disabled where not required for business operations. Where such capability is necessary, it operates only through approved, monitored channels.

subs.title: Prompt Access Termination on Departure
subs.description: When personnel separate from the company or transfer roles, their access to information systems and nonpublic information is terminated promptly. Offboarding workflows between HR and identity management ensure deprovisioning is not dependent on manual follow-up.

subs.title: Industry-Standard Password Policy and Class A PAM Controls
subs.description: A written password policy meeting industry standards governs credential length, complexity, reuse, and storage across the enterprise. As a Class A company, the carrier must additionally operate a privileged-access management solution and an automated method of blocking commonly used passwords for all accounts, or document CISO-approved compensating controls.

items.name: Annual Certification of Material Compliance
items.summary: Governs the carrier's annual filing obligation under 23 NYCRR 500.17(b), under which the company attests each year to the superintendent on its compliance posture for the prior calendar year. The standard ensures the attestation is evidence-backed, executive-accountable, and defensible in an examination.

subs.title: April 15 Certification or Acknowledgment Filing
subs.description: By April 15 each year the company must electronically submit either a Certification of Material Compliance, supported by sufficient data and documentation to substantiate the attestation, or a written Acknowledgment of noncompliance. An Acknowledgment must identify the sections not materially complied with, describe the nature and extent of the gaps, and provide a remediation timeline or confirmation that remediation is complete.

subs.title: Signed by the Highest-Ranking Executive and the CISO
subs.description: The filing must be signed by both the company's highest-ranking executive and its Chief Information Security Officer, placing personal accountability for the accuracy of the attestation at the top of the organization. Both signatories review the supporting compliance evidence before signing.

subs.title: Supporting Records Retained Five Years
subs.description: All records, schedules, and data supporting the certification or acknowledgment must be maintained for five years and produced to the superintendent on request. The retention obligation covers the underlying control evidence, not merely the filed document.

items.name: Application Security (Secure SDLC)
items.summary: Implements 23 NYCRR 500.8 by embedding security requirements into how the carrier builds, buys, and integrates application software. It ensures both internally developed and vendor-supplied applications that touch nonpublic information are engineered and evaluated against documented security standards.

subs.title: Written Secure-Development and External-Application Evaluation Procedures
subs.description: The cybersecurity program must include written procedures, guidelines, and standards for secure development of applications built in-house, covering practices such as secure coding requirements, security testing, and release gates. Equivalent written procedures must govern how the security of externally developed applications used by the company is evaluated, assessed, and tested before and during use.

subs.title: Annual Review by the CISO or Qualified Designee
subs.description: The application security procedures, guidelines, and standards must be reviewed, assessed, and updated as necessary at least annually by the CISO or a qualified designee. Reviews confirm the material remains current with the threat landscape, the technology stack, and findings from testing and incidents.

items.name: Asset Inventory
items.summary: Implements the 23 NYCRR 500.13(a) requirement to maintain written policies and procedures that produce and sustain a complete, accurate, and documented inventory of the carrier's information systems. For each asset the inventory must track, at minimum, the owner, location, classification or sensitivity, support-expiration date, and recovery-time objective, and the policies must define how frequently the inventory is updated and validated so it remains a reliable foundation for risk assessment, patching, and incident response.

items.name: Audit Trail
items.summary: Implements 23 NYCRR 500.6 by requiring the carrier to maintain, to the extent applicable and based on its risk assessment, systems designed to reconstruct material financial transactions sufficient to support normal operations and obligations, with those records retained for at least five years. It likewise requires audit trails designed to detect and respond to cybersecurity events that have a reasonable likelihood of materially harming any material part of normal operations, retained for at least three years.

items.name: Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery
items.summary: Implements the BCDR requirements of 23 NYCRR 500.16, ensuring the carrier can sustain or rapidly restore the information systems and services that policyholders, claims operations, and regulators depend on through a cyber disruption. The standard covers the full lifecycle of continuity planning, from asset identification through annual proof that recovery actually works.

subs.title: Written BCDR Plans Ensuring Availability of Systems and Material Services
subs.description: The incident response and BCDR program must include written plans reasonably designed to ensure the availability and functionality of the company's information systems and material services, and to protect personnel, assets, and nonpublic information in the event of a cybersecurity-related disruption. Plans address communications, succession, and procedures for timely recovery of critical data and systems.

subs.title: Identify Essential Assets and Personnel
subs.description: BCDR plans must identify the documents, data, facilities, infrastructure, services, and personnel essential to continued operations, along with the third parties necessary to recovery. Supervisory personnel responsible for implementing each part of the plan are designated by name or role.

subs.title: Protected Offsite Backups
subs.description: The company must maintain backups of information essential to its operations that are adequately protected from unauthorized alteration or destruction, including isolation or other safeguards against ransomware-style compromise, and stored offsite from the primary systems they protect.

subs.title: Plan Distribution and Training
subs.description: Current copies of the BCDR plans, or the relevant portions, must be accessible to all personnel needed to implement them, including during a disruption when normal systems may be unavailable. Relevant employees receive training on their plan responsibilities.

subs.title: Annual Testing of Plans and Backup Restoration
subs.description: The BCDR plans must be tested at least annually with the participation of senior officers and all staff critical to recovery, and the company must also test its ability to restore critical data and systems from backups at least annually. Test results feed revisions to the plans as necessary.

items.name: Cybersecurity Governance & CISO Oversight
items.summary: Implements the governance requirements of 23 NYCRR 500.4, establishing clear executive accountability for the carrier's cybersecurity program. It pairs a designated CISO with documented board-level oversight so cyber risk is managed and resourced as an enterprise concern rather than a delegated technical matter.

subs.title: Designated CISO With Annual and Timely Reporting
subs.description: A qualified individual must be designated as CISO, responsible for overseeing, implementing, and enforcing the cybersecurity program and policy. The CISO reports in writing at least annually to the senior governing body on the program and material cyber risks, and reports in a timely manner on material cybersecurity issues such as significant events or major program changes.

subs.title: Senior Governing Body Oversight of Cyber Risk
subs.description: The board or equivalent senior governing body must exercise documented oversight of cybersecurity risk management, including maintaining sufficient understanding of cyber matters, requiring executive management to develop and maintain the program, regularly reviewing management and CISO reports, and confirming the program is allocated adequate resources.

items.name: Cybersecurity Personnel & Intelligence
items.summary: Implements 23 NYCRR 500.10 by ensuring the carrier staffs its cybersecurity function with qualified people and keeps their knowledge current with the evolving threat environment. The standard applies whether security capability is delivered in-house, through an affiliate, or by an external provider.

subs.title: Qualified Cybersecurity Personnel Sufficient to Manage Risk
subs.description: The company must utilize qualified cybersecurity personnel, whether its own employees, affiliate staff, or a third-party service provider, sufficient to manage its cybersecurity risks and to perform or oversee the core functions of the cybersecurity program. Staffing adequacy is evaluated against the risk assessment rather than headcount alone.

subs.title: Cybersecurity Updates and Training for Security Personnel
subs.description: Cybersecurity personnel must be provided with updates and training sufficient to address relevant risks, keeping their skills aligned with the technologies the carrier operates and the threats it faces. Training plans are refreshed as the program and risk assessment evolve.

subs.title: Current Threat and Countermeasure Knowledge for Key Personnel
subs.description: The company must verify that key cybersecurity personnel take steps to maintain current knowledge of changing threats and countermeasures, for example through threat-intelligence consumption, professional certifications, and industry information-sharing participation. Verification is part of the personnel oversight process, not left to individual initiative.

items.name: Cybersecurity Policy
items.summary: Implements 23 NYCRR 500.3 by requiring the carrier to maintain written cybersecurity policies and procedures, approved at least annually by a senior officer or the senior governing body, for the protection of its information systems and the nonpublic information stored on them. The policies must address, to the extent applicable, the regulation's enumerated domains, including data governance, classification, and retention, asset inventory and device management, access controls, business continuity and disaster recovery, network security and monitoring, application security, vendor and third-party management, risk assessment, incident response, and vulnerability management.

items.name: Cybersecurity Program
items.summary: Implements 23 NYCRR 500.2 by requiring the carrier to maintain a cybersecurity program, based on its risk assessment, designed to protect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of its information systems. The program must perform the six core functions: identifying internal and external cyber risks, using defensive infrastructure to protect systems and nonpublic information, detecting cybersecurity events, responding to mitigate them, recovering and restoring normal operations, and fulfilling applicable regulatory reporting obligations; as a Class A company, the carrier must also design and conduct independent audits of the program based on its risk assessment.

items.name: Data Retention & Secure Disposal
items.summary: Implements 23 NYCRR 500.13(b) by requiring the carrier to maintain policies and procedures for the secure disposal, on a periodic basis, of nonpublic information in the personal-identifier and health-information categories that is no longer necessary for business operations or other legitimate business purposes. Disposal is excused only where the information must be retained by law or regulation, or where targeted disposal is not reasonably feasible because of how the information is maintained.

items.name: Encryption of Nonpublic Information
items.summary: Implements 23 NYCRR 500.15, requiring cryptographic protection of the policyholder, claimant, and business data that constitutes nonpublic information wherever it moves or rests. The standard ensures encryption decisions follow a written, industry-aligned policy and that any gaps are governed by formal CISO-approved exceptions rather than informal practice.

subs.title: Written Encryption Policy for NPI in Transit and at Rest
subs.description: The cybersecurity program must include a written encryption policy that meets industry standards and protects nonpublic information both in transit over external networks and at rest. The policy specifies approved algorithms, protocols, and key-management practices for systems handling NPI across the carrier's P&C, life and retirement, and group benefits operations.

subs.title: CISO-Approved Compensating Controls Where At-Rest Encryption Is Infeasible
subs.description: Where the company determines that encrypting NPI at rest is infeasible for a particular system, it may instead secure the data using effective alternative compensating controls that have been reviewed and approved in writing by the CISO. The feasibility determination and the effectiveness of each compensating control must be reviewed by the CISO at least annually.

items.name: Extortion / Ransomware Payment Notice
items.summary: Implements the extortion-payment notification duties of 23 NYCRR 500.17(c). If the carrier makes an extortion payment in connection with a cybersecurity event, it must notify the superintendent electronically within 24 hours of the payment, and within 30 days provide a written description of the reasons payment was necessary, the alternatives that were considered, all diligence performed to find alternatives, and the diligence performed to ensure the payment complied with applicable rules and regulations, including those of the Office of Foreign Assets Control.

items.name: Incident Response Plan
items.summary: Implements the incident response planning requirements of 23 NYCRR 500.16, ensuring the carrier can respond to and recover from cybersecurity events affecting its systems in a planned, practiced, and accountable manner. The standard defines what the written plan must contain, the disruptive scenarios it must contemplate, and how its readiness is proven.

subs.title: Written Plan Covering Processes, Authority, Communications, Remediation, Recovery, and Root Cause
subs.description: The company must maintain a written incident response plan addressing the goals of the plan, internal response processes, clear roles, responsibilities, and levels of decision-making authority, external and internal communications and information sharing, remediation of identified weaknesses, documentation and reporting of events and response activities, recovery from backups, and preparation of a root-cause analysis describing how the incident occurred and what is being changed to prevent recurrence.

subs.title: Coverage of Disruptive Events Such as Ransomware
subs.description: The plan must be reasonably designed to enable prompt response to and recovery from disruptive cybersecurity events, explicitly including ransomware incidents that could deny the carrier access to its systems or data. Scenario content addresses containment, restoration, and the regulatory notifications such events trigger.

subs.title: Annual Testing
subs.description: The incident response plan must be tested at least annually, with participation from senior officers and the staff critical to executing it, through exercises such as tabletop simulations. Lessons learned from tests and from actual incidents are incorporated into plan revisions.

items.name: Monitoring & Malicious-Code Protection
items.summary: Implements 23 NYCRR 500.14(a) and (b) by requiring risk-based policies, procedures, and controls designed to monitor the activity of authorized users and detect unauthorized access to, use of, or tampering with nonpublic information, together with protections against malicious code that include monitoring and filtering of web traffic and email. As a Class A company, the carrier must additionally implement an endpoint detection and response solution and a centralized solution for logging and security-event alerting, such as a SIEM, unless the CISO approves equivalent compensating controls in writing.

items.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
items.summary: Implements 23 NYCRR 500.12 by requiring multi-factor authentication for any individual accessing any of the carrier's information systems; entities qualifying for the limited exemption must apply MFA at minimum to remote access to systems, remote access to third-party applications from which nonpublic information is accessible, and all privileged accounts other than service accounts that prohibit interactive login. The CISO may approve in writing the use of reasonably equivalent or more secure compensating controls, which must be reviewed at least annually.

items.name: Nonpublic Information Classification
items.summary: Establishes how the carrier identifies and classifies the data that qualifies as Nonpublic Information under 23 NYCRR 500.1, so that the regulation's access, encryption, retention, monitoring, and audit-trail controls are applied to the right systems and records. Accurate NPI classification is the foundation on which the rest of the Part 500 program is scoped.

subs.title: Material Business Information
subs.description: Classification must capture business-related information whose unauthorized disclosure, access, or use would cause a material adverse impact to the company's business, operations, or security. This category covers items such as material non-public financial data, strategic plans, and sensitive operational details, independent of any personal data content.

subs.title: Personal Identifiers Combined With Sensitive Data Elements
subs.description: Information concerning an individual must be classified as NPI when a name, number, mark, or other identifier appears in combination with elements such as a Social Security number, driver's license or non-driver ID number, financial account, credit, or debit card number, security or access codes or passwords permitting account access, or biometric records. Carrier systems holding policyholder, claimant, and employee records are mapped against these combinations.

subs.title: Health Information and Control Scoping
subs.description: Health-related information created by or derived from a health care provider or the individual, relating to physical, mental, or behavioral health, care provision, or payment for care, must also be classified as NPI, a category especially significant for the life, disability, and group benefits businesses. Classification results drive the scoping of access, encryption, retention, monitoring, and audit-trail controls across the affected systems.

items.name: Risk Assessment
items.summary: Implements 23 NYCRR 500.9 by making a documented enterprise cyber risk assessment the engine that drives the design of the carrier's cybersecurity program and controls. The standard governs both the conduct of the assessment and the cadence on which it must be refreshed.

subs.title: Documented Periodic Risk Assessment Informing the Program
subs.description: The company must conduct a periodic risk assessment of its information systems, carried out in accordance with written policies and procedures and documented in full. The assessment evaluates threats, the adequacy of existing controls, and how identified risks will be mitigated or accepted, and its results inform the design of the cybersecurity program.

subs.title: Annual Update and Refresh on Material Change
subs.description: The risk assessment must be reviewed and updated at least annually, and additionally whenever a change in the business or in technology causes a material change to the company's cyber risk, such as an acquisition, a major platform migration, or adoption of a new distribution channel. Updates address new threats and ensure the program keeps pace with the carrier's actual exposure.

items.name: Security Awareness Training
items.summary: Implements 23 NYCRR 500.14(a)(3) by requiring the carrier to provide cybersecurity awareness training to all personnel periodically, and at least annually. The training must include social engineering content, such as phishing and pretexting exercises, and must be updated to reflect the risks identified in the company's most recent risk assessment so the curriculum tracks the threats the workforce actually faces.

items.name: Third-Party Service Provider Security
items.summary: Implements 23 NYCRR 500.11, governing how the carrier manages the cyber risk introduced by the vendors, administrators, and service providers that access its systems or hold its nonpublic information. The standard ensures provider risk is assessed before engagement, codified in contracts, and revisited over the life of the relationship.

subs.title: Written TPSP Policies: Identification, Risk Assessment, Due Diligence, and Reassessment
subs.description: The company must maintain written policies and procedures addressing the identification and risk assessment of third-party service providers with access to its information systems or nonpublic information, the minimum cybersecurity practices those providers must meet, due diligence processes to evaluate the adequacy of each provider's practices, and periodic reassessment of providers based on the risk they present. For an insurer this spans TPAs, reinsurance intermediaries, agency platforms, and technology vendors alike.

subs.title: Contractual Guidelines on Provider MFA, Encryption, and Breach Notice
subs.description: The TPSP policies must include relevant guidelines for due diligence and contractual protections addressing, to the extent applicable, the provider's use of multi-factor authentication, its use of encryption to protect nonpublic information in transit and at rest, and its obligation to provide notice to the company of cybersecurity events directly affecting the carrier's systems or NPI. These requirements are embedded in contract templates and verified during vendor reviews.

items.name: Vulnerability Management
items.summary: Implements 23 NYCRR 500.5 by requiring written policies and procedures, developed in accordance with the risk assessment, that keep vulnerabilities in the carrier's information systems identified and remediated on a defensible cadence. The policies must ensure penetration testing of systems from both inside and outside their boundaries by a qualified internal or external party at least annually, automated scans plus manual review of systems the scans cannot cover at a frequency determined by the risk assessment and promptly after any material system change, a documented process for monitoring sources of newly disclosed vulnerabilities, and timely remediation prioritized by risk; as a Class A company, external experts must be involved in the testing program.

items.name: Data Flow & Trust Boundaries
items.summary: Requires that every data flow between systems, networks, and external parties be documented with its trust boundary classifications, so the architecture team can see where data crosses from higher-trust to lower-trust zones. Maintained data flow diagrams identify the sources, destinations, transport mechanisms, and boundary crossings for sensitive data such as policyholder NPI, giving security reviews, threat models, and regulatory responses an authoritative picture of where controls must sit.

items.name: Defense in Depth Strategy
items.summary: Requires multiple independent layers of security controls across the network, application, data, and endpoint tiers, so that the failure or bypass of any single control does not expose the carrier's systems or nonpublic information. Architects must demonstrate in design reviews that each critical asset is protected by overlapping controls, such as network segmentation and firewalls, application-level authentication and input validation, data encryption and access governance, and endpoint protection and hardening, rather than relying on a single perimeter.

items.name: Security Reference Architecture
items.summary: Establishes standard, pre-approved security patterns for cloud deployments, covering constructs such as VPC design, subnet segmentation, and security group rules, as well as for on-premises and hybrid environments. Project teams build from these published reference patterns rather than designing security topology from scratch, which keeps controls consistent across the carrier's P&C, Life & Retirement, and group benefits platforms and shortens architecture review cycles.

items.name: Threat Modeling (STRIDE)
items.summary: Requires every new system to complete a STRIDE threat modeling exercise, analyzing spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, and elevation of privilege threats, before its design can be approved. The resulting threat model documents identified threats, their mitigations, and accepted residual risks, and serves as a gate in the architecture review process so security weaknesses are addressed in design rather than discovered in production.

items.name: Zero Trust Architecture Model
items.summary: Establishes zero trust as the carrier's network access model, replacing implicit trust in the corporate network perimeter with continuous verification of every user, device, and connection. The model protects policy administration, claims, and data platforms even when an attacker has already gained a foothold inside the environment.

subs.title: Assume Breach for All Network Access
subs.description: All network access must be designed on the assumption that the environment is already compromised, so no connection is trusted simply because it originates inside the corporate network. Architectures favor segmentation, encrypted internal traffic, and continuous monitoring that limit lateral movement and blast radius when a breach occurs.

subs.title: Verify Explicitly With Least Privilege
subs.description: Every access request must be explicitly authenticated and authorized using all available signals, including user identity, device health, location, and the sensitivity of the requested resource, with access granted at the least privilege necessary and re-evaluated rather than persisting indefinitely. Designs incorporate the assume-breach posture throughout, applying just-in-time and just-enough access for administrative functions.

items.name: Alert Thresholds & Tuning
items.summary: Governs how detection alerting in the security operations center is calibrated and maintained, so analysts spend their time on genuine threats to the carrier's systems rather than noise. The standard pairs documented thresholds with a measurable quality target for alert fidelity.

subs.title: Quarterly Documented Threshold Tuning
subs.description: Alert thresholds for each detection rule must be documented, including the rationale for the configured values, and reviewed and tuned at least quarterly. Tuning sessions incorporate recent incident findings, changes to the environment, and analyst feedback, and all threshold changes are recorded with approval and effective date.

subs.title: False Positive Rate Below 10 Percent
subs.description: The alerting program must maintain a false positive rate below 10 percent, measured from analyst triage dispositions. Detection rules that exceed the threshold are flagged for retuning or retirement, and the metric is reported as part of security operations performance reviews.

items.name: Log Retention
items.summary: Establishes the tiered retention schedule for security logs across the enterprise: 90 days in hot storage for immediate search and active investigation, one year in warm storage for trend analysis and slower-burn investigations, and seven years in archive to satisfy compliance and regulatory obligations, including insurance-sector examination and audit-trail requirements. All log sources feeding the security tooling must conform to this schedule, and archived logs must remain retrievable for the full retention period.

items.name: SIEM Integration
items.summary: Requires every application across the carrier's portfolio to feed the enterprise security monitoring platform, giving the security operations center timely, centralized visibility into events from policy, claims, billing, and corporate systems alike. The standard fixes both the destination for security telemetry and the freshness it must achieve.

subs.title: All Applications Log to the Enterprise SIEM
subs.description: Every application, whether built in-house, purchased, or SaaS, must ship its security-relevant logs to the enterprise SIEM platform (Sentinel or Splunk). Onboarding to the SIEM is a go-live requirement, with log source, format, and parsing validated by the security operations team before production release.

subs.title: Log Shipping Within Five Minutes
subs.description: Security events must arrive in the SIEM within five minutes of generation, so detection rules and analyst investigations operate on near-real-time data. Log pipeline latency is monitored, and sources that fall behind the five-minute target generate operational alerts for remediation.

items.name: Security Event Logging
items.summary: Defines the minimum set of security-relevant events that every system must capture: authentication attempts, authorization decisions, access to data, and configuration changes. Logging these categories consistently across applications and infrastructure gives the carrier the evidence needed to detect unauthorized activity against policyholder data, support incident investigations, and demonstrate control operation to auditors and regulators.

items.name: Security Playbooks
items.summary: Ensures the security operations team responds to its highest-volume alert types through documented, repeatable procedures rather than analyst improvisation. The standard covers both the creation of playbooks for the most common alerts and the regular exercising that keeps them effective.

subs.title: Documented Playbooks for the Top 20 Security Alerts
subs.description: Written response playbooks must exist for the 20 most frequent or highest-impact security alert types, each defining triage steps, investigation queries, containment actions, escalation criteria, and closure requirements. Playbooks are maintained in the SOC knowledge base and updated as detection content and the environment change.

subs.title: Quarterly Playbook Testing
subs.description: Each playbook must be exercised at least quarterly, through live alert handling, simulation, or tabletop walkthrough, to confirm the documented steps still work against current tooling and system configurations. Gaps identified during testing are remediated and the playbook revised with a record of the test date and outcome.

items.name: Patch Management SLA
items.summary: Sets the maximum remediation timelines for applying security patches based on vulnerability severity: critical vulnerabilities within 72 hours, high within 7 days, medium within 30 days, and low within 90 days. The clock starts when the vulnerability is confirmed applicable to the carrier's environment, and SLA compliance is tracked and reported so unpatched exposure on systems handling policyholder data is bounded and visible to management.

items.name: Penetration Testing
items.summary: Defines the offensive-testing regime that validates the carrier's defenses against realistic attack techniques, complementing automated scanning with human-driven exploitation attempts. The standard combines independent external testing of the enterprise with a faster internal cycle focused on the systems that matter most.

subs.title: Annual Third-Party Penetration Test
subs.description: An independent third-party firm must conduct a penetration test of the carrier's environment at least annually, with scope covering externally facing and key internal systems. Findings are risk-rated, tracked to remediation, and the engagement reports are retained as evidence for regulatory and audit requirements, including NYDFS testing expectations.

subs.title: Quarterly Internal Penetration Testing of Critical Systems
subs.description: Systems classified as critical, such as policy administration, claims, and payment platforms, must undergo internal penetration testing each quarter, performed by the internal security testing team. The higher cadence ensures changes to these systems are probed for exploitable weaknesses well before the next external engagement.

items.name: Remediation Tracking
items.summary: Ensures that serious vulnerability findings are managed to verified closure rather than left in scanner reports, with a formal governance path for any that cannot be fixed on schedule. The standard makes remediation status auditable and exception decisions accountable at the executive level.

subs.title: Critical and High Vulnerabilities Tracked to Closure
subs.description: Every critical and high severity vulnerability must be recorded in the remediation tracking system with an assigned owner, target date aligned to the patching SLA, and current status, and remains open until the fix is verified by rescan or retest. Aging items are escalated through the vulnerability management governance process.

subs.title: Exceptions Require CISO Approval
subs.description: Any deviation from required remediation, whether a deferral, a compensating control in place of a fix, or formal risk acceptance, must be approved by the CISO. Approved exceptions are documented with justification, compensating measures, and an expiration date that forces re-review rather than permitting indefinite exposure.

items.name: Vulnerability Scanning Cadence
items.summary: Fixes the minimum frequency at which the carrier's estate is scanned for known vulnerabilities, weighting effort toward the environments where exploitation would directly affect policyholders and operations. Scan coverage and schedule adherence are monitored as core vulnerability-program metrics.

subs.title: Weekly Scans for All Production Systems
subs.description: Every production system must be scanned for vulnerabilities at least weekly using authenticated scans wherever technically feasible, ensuring newly disclosed flaws in internet-facing and core insurance platforms are identified within days. Missed or failed scans are treated as coverage gaps and remediated promptly.

subs.title: Monthly Scans for Non-Production Systems
subs.description: Non-production environments, including development, test, and staging systems, must be scanned at least monthly. The cadence recognizes their lower direct exposure while still catching vulnerable components before they promote to production and preventing non-prod from becoming an unmonitored foothold.
